nature-eco-276.q: What is the difference between infiltration-excess and saturation-excess runoff?
nature-eco-276.a: Infiltration excess happens when rain is too intense or soils are sealed, as in drylands and paved areas; saturation excess happens when rain keeps falling on soil already full of water.

nature-eco-219.q: How can harmful algal blooms threaten people?
nature-eco-219.a: Dying or eaten algae release nerve and liver toxins, which can reach people through shellfish poisoning.

nature-eco-225.q: Why can recovery from eutrophication take a long time?
nature-eco-225.a: Nutrients stored in sediments keep being released, and a water body can have several stable but very different states.

nature-eco-267.q: What causes eroded hilltops in farm fields?
nature-eco-267.a: Tillage, since water erosion removes soil mainly from mid and lower slopes.

nature-eco-229.q: How can evapotranspiration be worked out from a catchment water balance?
nature-eco-229.a: The balance relates the change in stored water to precipitation, evapotranspiration, streamflow and groundwater recharge, so evapotranspiration can be solved for.

nature-eco-208.q: Where does the dissolved organic carbon in the microbial loop come from?
nature-eco-208.a: From bursting bacteria, leakage from phytoplankton, sloppy feeding by zooplankton and animal wastes.

nature-eco-247.q: How do load-oriented and source-oriented approaches to pollution apportionment differ?
nature-eco-247.a: Load-oriented ones work back from stream monitoring data; source-oriented ones model emissions using figures from similar catchments.

nature-eco-197.q: Where is most of Earth's fresh water?
nature-eco-197.a: In ice caps, glaciers and permanent snow, which hold 68.7% of all fresh water.

nature-eco-236.q: Why can lakes run short of oxygen in winter?
nature-eco-236.a: Ice and snow cut light for photosynthesis and block oxygen exchange with the air while respiration continues.

nature-eco-211.a: It frees the energy stored in organic molecules and recycles matter as nutrients for other organisms.

nature-eco-187.q: How has the ratio of nitrogen to phosphorus changed, and with what effect?
nature-eco-187.a: It has risen over the last 40 years, leaving phosphorus less available to ecosystems.

nature-eco-231.q: Why has synthetic fertilizer been called the detonator of the population explosion?
nature-eco-231.a: It helped world population grow from 1.6 billion in 1900 to 7.7 billion by 2018.

nature-clim-206.q: Why is it hard to tell whether ocean iron fertilization stores more carbon?
nature-clim-206.a: The ocean is vast and consumers respond quickly to extra growth.

nature-eco-254.q: What does a rising Revelle factor mean for the ocean's uptake of carbon dioxide?
nature-eco-254.a: The lower the factor, the more CO2 water can take in; it rises as CO2 rises, so the ocean will take a smaller share of human emissions.

nature-eco-233.q: What harm can extra nitrogen deposition do?
nature-eco-233.a: It can acidify soils, streams and lakes and change forest and grassland productivity.

nature-eco-162.q: Which gases in air absorb heat radiation, and which barely do?
nature-eco-162.a: Nitrogen and oxygen barely absorb it, while CO2, methane and nitrous oxide do, producing the greenhouse effect.

nature-eco-017.q: Why do climate tipping points matter?
nature-eco-017.a: Some changes can become irreversible once tipping points are crossed.

nature-eco-009.q: How cold would Earth's surface be without the natural greenhouse effect?
nature-eco-009.a: About −18 °C on average instead of around 15 °C.

nature-eco-012.q: When does the IPCC expect average warming to pass +1.5 °C?
nature-eco-012.a: In the early 2030s, measured as a 20-year average.

nature-eco-019.q: How does climate change harm food production?
nature-eco-019.a: Through higher CO2, heat, changed rainfall, more extreme events and shifting pests and diseases.

nature-eco-008.q: What does the strength of the CO2 fertilization effect depend on?
nature-eco-008.a: Plant species, temperature and the water and nutrients available.

nature-eco-129.q: What drives humanity's global-scale damage to the environment?
nature-eco-129.a: Population growth, rapid economic growth, overconsumption, overexploitation, pollution and deforestation.

nature-eco-026.q: Which non-native species count as invasive?
nature-eco-026.a: Established non-native species that threaten native species and biodiversity.

nature-eco-091.q: What is the immediate cause of desertification?
nature-eco-091.a: The loss of most vegetation, driven by drought, climate shifts, tillage, overgrazing and cutting trees.

nature-eco-069.q: What does relative species abundance compare?
nature-eco-069.a: One species' abundance with that of others in the ecosystem.

nature-eco-123.q: How many species did the IPBES global assessment find threatened with extinction?
nature-eco-123.a: 1 million of an estimated 8 million animal and plant species.

nature-eco-056.q: Why do forest owners often overlook many forest functions?
nature-eco-056.a: Many important functions have no markets and so no readily apparent economic value.

nature-eco-027.q: How has the economic cost of invasive species changed over time?
nature-eco-027.a: It has quadrupled every decade since 1970, exceeding $423 billion a year as of 2019.

nature-eco-099.q: How do species mainly become endangered?
nature-eco-099.a: Through habitat loss and loss of genetic variation.

nature-eco-022.q: How fast are species now disappearing compared with the natural rate?
nature-eco-022.a: An estimated 100 to 1,000 times faster than the natural background extinction rate.

nature-eco-131.q: How does in situ conservation differ from ex situ conservation?
nature-eco-131.a: In situ protects species where they live, in places like reserves and parks; ex situ keeps them or their material elsewhere, as in seed libraries and gene banks.

nature-eco-054.a: The conversion of forest to other land uses, whether or not people caused it.

nature-eco-040.q: Why are freshwater ecosystems so important for biodiversity?
nature-eco-040.a: They cover 1% of Earth's surface but are home to about one third of vertebrate species.

nature-eco-029.q: Which body oversees the Ballast Water Management Convention?

nature-eco-074.q: Why are seed banks considered a fairly reliable way to keep genetic diversity?
nature-eco-074.a: Stored material changes little over the long term.

nature-eco-101.q: Why has private rhino farming helped rhino numbers?
nature-eco-101.a: Ecotourism and sales give owners strong incentives to look after rhinos rather than poach them.

nature-eco-108.q: What does the rediscovery of the coelacanth show about extinction?
nature-eco-108.a: How hard it is to establish exactly when a species has gone extinct; it was found alive in 1938 after being known only from fossils.

nature-eco-024.q: What has been the main cause of mammal extinctions since the Late Pleistocene?
nature-eco-024.a: Human activity; megafaunal extinctions correlate with the arrival of humans.

nature-eco-092.q: What is now thought to mainly cause drought in the Sahel?
nature-eco-092.a: Rainfall variability driven by ocean temperatures, aerosols and greenhouse gases, rather than overgrazing as early studies claimed.

nature-mkt-009.q: What did a review of fragmentation effects suggest about one large versus several small reserves?
nature-mkt-009.a: Most significant effects of fragmentation itself were positive, implying several small patches can sometimes beat one large one.

nature-eco-071.q: What are the limits of DAFOR and ACFOR ratings?
nature-eco-071.a: They give rough estimates but are not exact or objective, so better methods should be used where available.

nature-eco-076.q: In Whittaker's scheme, what does total landscape diversity depend on?
nature-eco-076.a: On local diversity (alpha) and on how much sites differ (beta).

nature-eco-067.q: How does deforestation affect local climate?
nature-eco-067.a: Reduced rainfall brings a hotter, drier climate, longer dry seasons, more fires and disrupted pollination.

nature-eco-148.q: What happens to Hill-number diversity as q is raised?
nature-eco-148.a: More weight goes to the most abundant species, so larger q gives lower diversity for the same data; at q = 0 it equals species richness.

nature-eco-085.q: How did falling fish stocks in Ghana affect wildlife?
nature-eco-085.a: People turned to hunting animals in nature reserves, and wildlife declines were tied to a falling fish supply.

nature-eco-155.q: What is the case for a regulated legal wildlife trade, and what is its main obstacle?
nature-eco-155.a: It could push down illegal prices, cutting the incentive to poach, or raise conservation money; laundering and corruption are major obstacles.

nature-eco-111.q: Why is extinction debt hard to measure?
nature-eco-111.a: The processes are slow and noisy and tiny remnant populations are hard to count, so estimates are very uncertain.

nature-acct-088.q: What does this index show about local land biodiversity?
nature-acct-088.a: How it responds to pressures such as land-use change and intensification.

nature-eco-031.q: What role are introduced Aldabra giant tortoises playing on islets off Mauritius?
nature-eco-031.a: They are replacing extinct native tortoises as seed dispersers and grazers of invasive plants.

nature-eco-117.q: In Whittaker's view, what sets gamma diversity?
nature-eco-117.a: The average diversity of local sites (alpha) and how much those sites differ (beta).
